name: Driftpile Acidwalk Full Kit
description: Built around a rubberized poncho-coat in matte black that has long since faded to an uneven charcoal, this outfit is a the Gray Zone rain-walker's solution to the Great Lakes acid season. The poncho-coat reaches mid-thigh, its hem patched in four places with strips of bright yellow hazard tape that the wearer has made no attempt to hide — they're functional and they're a statement. Beneath it, a dense-knit compression top in dark teal, faded nearly to gray at the shoulders, sits tucked into wide-leg work trousers in heavyweight stained canvas, olive-brown, with a drawstring waist because the original button hardware gave out. The trousers have a gene-compatible rear seam — split and re-hemmed with elastic to accommodate a tail or lower-back geneware — suggesting the wearer either has modifications or bought the trousers secondhand from someone who did. Boots are tall and utilitarian: knee-high salvage pulls in cracked synthetic leather, resoled with thick rubber compound that smells faintly of chemical treatment, the inner lining replaced with cut-up foam insulation. Hands are covered by fingerless gloves in worn leather, the knuckles patched with embedded rubber nodes stripped from industrial grip-tape. A wide-brimmed hat in stiff waxed canvas, acid-pocked but holding shape, completes the silhouette — shaped and battered into a permanent slight lean to one side.
functionality: Rubberized poncho-coat sheds acid rain and light chemical splash. Tall synthetic boots protect lower legs from flood-water and chemical runoff. Grip-tape knuckle gloves improve hold on wet or slick surfaces. Wide-brimmed hat keeps acid rain off face and neck. Gene-compatible trouser seam accommodates tail-bearing wearers.
what_it_says: Someone who moves through the Gray Zone's worst weather conditions regularly and has engineered their wardrobe to survive it. The yellow hazard tape hem is defiant — practical necessity worn like a badge. The secondhand gene-compatible trousers suggest a community that shares and adapts.
manufacturer: Poncho-coat is a Floodline industrial surplus second; remaining components are self-modified or sourced from the Gray Zone market vendors
story_hooks: The chemical treatment on the boot resoles is a proprietary formula the wearer mixed themselves — and a Tier 3 materials chemist has noticed it's better than anything commercially available.

The gene-compatible trouser seam is stitched in a specific pattern that marks the wearer as belonging to a particular the Gray Zone mutual-aid collective — which makes them a target for a rival group.
During a sudden acid downpour, the wearer is the only person on the street prepared to move safely — and someone desperate needs an escort to the nearest shelter.

physical_description.visual_profile: A rain-walker's silhouette: broad and protective, built for chemical exposure and street survival. The matte charcoal poncho-coat dominates, creating a loose, enveloping shape that reads utilitarian and deliberately unglamorous. Layered beneath are faded teal compression and olive work trousers that suggest practical modification over time. The overall impression is weathered, functional, and marked by visible repair—someone who exists in the acid-season gutters of the GLMZ and makes no apology for it.
physical_description.fit: Loose and oversized through the poncho-coat; compression top fitted but tucked; work trousers wide-leg and relaxed, held by drawstring. The ensemble is designed for mobility and chemical protection, not aesthetics. Tall boots provide rigid structural support.
physical_description.primary_material: Rubberized synthetic (poncho-coat), dense-knit synth-wool blend (compression top), heavyweight canvas (trousers), cracked synthetic leather with rubber-compound resole (boots), waxed canvas (hat), worn leather with embedded grip-tape (gloves)
physical_description.texture: Matte and slightly tacky (poncho-coat); fine ribbed knit (compression top); rough, heavy weave (trousers); cracked and weathered (boot leather); stiff, wax-stiffened (hat); callused leather with hard rubber nodes (gloves). Every surface reads as reconditioned and broken-in.
physical_description.color_scheme: Dominant matte charcoal with uneven fading; accents of bright yellow hazard tape (four patches on hem); dark teal compression faded to gray-teal; olive-brown canvas with stains and discoloration; black and tan leather; matte tan waxed canvas with acid pitting. High-contrast utility aesthetic.
physical_description.closures: Poncho-coat: friction-fit and overlap; trousers: drawstring waist; boots: lace-up (weathered cord); gloves: friction-fit pull-on; hat: none
distinctive_features: Four bright yellow hazard-tape patches on poncho-coat hem — functional and defiant
Gene-compatible rear seam with elastic gusset on trousers — signals geneware modification or secondhand origin
Fingerless gloves with embedded industrial grip-tape rubber nodes on knuckles
Knee-high salvage boots with thick chemical-treated rubber resole and foam-insulation lining replacement
Wide-brimmed waxed-canvas hat, acid-pocked, shaped with permanent lean
Visible patches, fading, and wear throughout — no attempt at repair concealment
physical_description.tier_indicator: Tier 5 salvage / sub-grade street wear. Every component is sourced from industrial surplus, secondhand markets, or self-modification. The outfit signals someone outside corpo infrastructure, built from what the Gray Zone economy provides.
physical_description.cultural_context: Acid-season rain-walker; the Gray Zone market denizen; likely geneware-modded; someone who walks toxic gutters and chemical runoff zones for work or survival. The visible modifications and hazard tape suggest someone proud of their survival adaptation rather than ashamed of their tier.
physical_description.condition_typical: Weathered, patched, faded, and broken-in. This outfit is not pristine—it is lived-in, chemically exposed, and showing its age. Wear is the point. Pristine condition would signal this is a fake or unused.
